records.title: Chewing gum caffeine enhances working memory speed in healthy young adults: a double-blind crossover trial
records.abstract: In this double-blind crossover study, 48 healthy adults aged 20-30 chewed caffeine gum (100 mg) or placebo. Working memory reaction times were significantly faster after caffeine (p = .008), quantified as mean latency on a 2-back task.

records.title: Habitual caffeine intake and working memory in a prospective cohort of university adults
records.abstract: We followed 412 university adults (aged 18-25) for 12 months. Habitual caffeine intake was positively associated with working memory span (beta = 0.21, p = .003), quantified via complex span tasks.

records.title: Acute caffeine ingestion improves working memory in adults: a randomized controlled trial (preprint version)
records.abstract: Preprint. In this double-blind randomized controlled trial, 60 healthy adults received 200 mg caffeine or placebo. The caffeine group showed significantly improved n-back working memory accuracy (p < .01).

records.title: Acute caffeine ingestion improves working memory performance in healthy adults: a randomized controlled trial
records.abstract: In this double-blind randomized controlled trial, 60 healthy adults aged 18-35 received 200 mg caffeine or placebo. The caffeine group showed significantly improved n-back working memory accuracy (p < .01), quantified as d' scores. This is the peer-reviewed published version.

records.title: Caffeine effects on working memory in older and younger adults: a controlled experiment
records.abstract: We tested 30 younger adults (aged 18-30) and 20 older adults (aged 65-80) on an n-back task after caffeine vs placebo. Working memory accuracy improved in younger adults (p = .02) but not in older adults (p = .44).

records.title: Caffeine, adenosine receptors and short-term memory: a brief report
Caffeine and cognition: a narrative review of the evidence
records.abstract: This narrative review summarizes 15 years of research on caffeine and cognition, including working memory, attention and executive function. It does not report new empirical data.
